tldr: Instead of two-phase distillation from a privileged teacher, the proposed method "Drift" freezes a pretrained vision encoder and performs direct visual reinforcement learning (one-phase) straight from images. It achieved a 58.8% relative improvement in real-world success rate over conventional approaches and showed strong robustness to unseen environments.
hero_caption: Comparison between two-phase distillation using privileged state information (left) and the proposed one-phase visual reinforcement learning method, "Drift" (right). Without relying on a teacher model, Drift directly trains a visual control policy with RL from images using a frozen vision backbone and lightweight Attention Pooling.
overview:
Sim-to-real reinforcement learning, which trains policies in simulation and deploys them to physical robots, has achieved remarkable success in robotic motor skills. However, when building visual policies that take camera images as input, the standard practice has been "two-phase distillation": first training a teacher policy via RL using internal simulation states (privileged information), and then having an image-based student policy imitate the teacher's actions. This approach suffers from fundamental issues, such as the "realizability gap" where the teacher relies on information unobservable by the student, as well as the inherent vulnerability of imitation learning to out-of-distribution shifts in the real world.

While running direct RL from image inputs from the start seems like the natural alternative, learning feature representations from scratch incurs prohibitive computational costs, making it practically intractable. To address this, the authors devised a simple framework called "Drift." It freezes a pretrained vision foundation model (ViT) to fix visual feature extraction, letting RL focus entirely on learning the control policy. Omitting backpropagation through the encoder dramatically accelerates training, while lightweight Attention Pooling efficiently aggregates the local features essential for contact-rich manipulation.

Under matched compute budgets and model capacities, Drift decisively outperformed two-phase distillation upon real-world deployment, despite showing comparable success rates in simulation. It achieved an average relative improvement of 58.8% across three real-world manipulation tasks. Furthermore, in controlled in-simulation distribution shift experiments, Drift maintained a 61% higher success rate under out-of-distribution conditions. The results reveal that policies acquired through direct RL possess an inherently stronger robustness to distribution shifts compared to students trained via imitation.
contributions: Proposed Drift, a simple one-phase visual RL recipe that optimizes policies directly from images by combining a frozen pretrained vision encoder with lightweight Attention Pooling.

Uncovered the "generalization gap" through controlled simulation evaluations under distribution shifts, demonstrating that one-phase visual RL maintains a roughly 61% higher success rate in out-of-distribution environments compared to two-phase distillation.

Demonstrated a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate over compute-matched two-phase distillation across three physical manipulation tasks: peg insertion, pushing, and cube picking.
Showed strong zero-shot adaptation capabilities to unseen objects with novel visual appearances and geometries, without any additional fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Why train directly with visual RL instead of two-phase distillation?
sections.summary: Privileged teacher-student distillation, the standard in conventional sim-to-real transfer, suffers from information asymmetry and poor real-world generalization. This work demonstrates that by leveraging frozen pretrained encoders, a one-phase approach training directly from images substantially outperforms distillation in both real-world transfer and out-of-distribution robustness.
sections.details:
Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has driven dramatic progress in robot locomotion and dexterous manipulation. However, many past successes relied on compact state observations, such as object poses estimated via carefully engineered perception pipelines.

To deploy policies directly from physical camera images, "two-phase distillation" has been widely adopted in practice. First, an expert teacher policy is trained via RL using privileged simulation information (such as exact object positions and velocities). Then, an image-based student policy is taught to imitate its behavior via imitation learning (such as DAgger). Yet, this pipeline hides two major pitfalls. First is the "realizability gap," where the teacher depends on privileged states that cannot be inferred from the student's camera views. Second, student policies trained via imitation are notoriously brittle to the domain shifts between simulation and reality. As a result, policies that appear highly capable in simulation often suffer severe performance drops when brought onto physical hardware.

Switching to "one-phase visual RL," which trains directly with image inputs from the outset, should solve these problems. However, learning visual representations and robot control simultaneously from scratch requires an enormous volume of samples and wall-clock time. To overcome this hurdle, this study introduces "Drift," a framework that freezes a pretrained vision foundation model (ViT) as a fixed feature extractor, concentrating all computational resources strictly on control learning. Combined with fast, rasterized simulation rendering, the authors discovered that Drift produces policies with far superior real-world transfer compared to two-phase distillation under identical compute budgets.

captions.F2: Architectural comparison between privileged two-phase distillation (left) and the proposed one-phase visual reinforcement learning (right). Drift bypasses the teacher model entirely. It trains the behavioral policy end-to-end using an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup—providing privileged state information only to the Critic during training—and a frozen ViT.

sections.heading: Prior work: From teacher-student distillation to frozen representations
sections.summary: While distillation from privileged teachers has seen many successes, performance degradation caused by information asymmetry remains a persistent issue. Meanwhile, GPU-accelerated parallel rendering and frozen pretrained representations have made direct visual RL practical, and this paper extends them to contact-rich manipulation tasks.
sections.details:
This study builds upon three major lines of related work.

First is the "teacher-student distillation" paradigm. Widely utilized in multi-fingered hand manipulation and humanoid control, it has persistently faced the "realizability gap" due to the discrepancy between the privileged state of the teacher and the visual inputs of the student. While previous work attempted co-training schemes that penalize divergence or used intermediate modalities like depth images, this study bypasses distillation altogether, learning directly from raw RGB images.

Second is the stream of "efficient visual RL and frozen representations." The advent of modern GPU-accelerated parallel simulators has significantly lowered the runtime barrier for direct visual RL. Furthermore, instead of training visual encoders from scratch, using fixed (frozen) weights from pretrained foundation models like DINOv2 has gained strong traction in domains like visual navigation. This paper extends this strategy to contact-rich manipulation tasks requiring millimeter-level precision, introducing a trainable Attention Pooling layer over patch features to preserve fine-grained spatial resolution.

Third is the "generalization difference between reinforcement learning and supervised learning." Recent research on foundation models highlights that RL post-training preserves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization far better than supervised fine-tuning. This paper validates this insight in sim-to-real robotic control: under controlled experimental setups, direct RL optimization is inherently more robust to disturbances and domain shifts than imitation-based distillation.

sections.heading: Formulation: How direct visual RL and two-phase distillation differ
sections.summary: Direct visual RL optimizes the policy to maximize expected future returns straight from image observations. In contrast, two-phase distillation trains the student policy using a supervised loss to mimic the actions of a privileged teacher, creating a fundamental divergence in their learning objectives.
sections.details:
At each time step $t$, the robot receives an observation $o_{t}=(I_{t},p_{t})$ consisting of an RGB image $I_{t}$ and proprioceptive states $p_{t}$ such as joint angles, and predicts a continuous action $a_{t}$. This paper mathematically contrasts the two competing paradigms for deriving visual policies from simulation.

### III-A Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning (1-Phase)
In direct visual RL, the policy $\pi_{\theta}(a_{t} \mid o_{t})$ directly maximizes the expected discounted cumulative return under the trajectory distribution it generates in simulation. In short, parameter updates for $\theta$ evaluate action values based on whether the action actually achieved the downstream task (outcome accountability).

### III-B Two-Phase Policy Distillation (2-Phase)
In two-phase distillation, an RL teacher policy $\pi_{T}(a_{t} \mid s_{t}^{\mathrm{priv}})$ is first trained using privileged simulator states $s_{t}^{\mathrm{priv}}$, such as ground-truth object poses and velocities. In the second phase, a vision-based student policy $\pi_{S,\theta}(a_{t} \mid o_{t})$ is trained. Under the DAgger-style distillation used in this work, the current student collects rollouts in the environment, and the frozen teacher labels each step with reference actions $a_{t}^{T}$. The student is then updated via supervised learning to minimize action discrepancy (e.g., mean squared error). The student does not maximize its own task return; it merely learns to copy the teacher, which is a fundamentally different objective.

sections.heading: Drift's design: Trimming computational waste with frozen foundation models
sections.summary: The proposed method, Drift, builds on an asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture with PPO while keeping the visual encoder completely frozen. Paired with lightweight Multihead Attention Pooling (MAP), it maximizes computational throughput without sacrificing fine-grained spatial patch features.
sections.details:
The architecture and training pipeline of Drift (Direct Reinforcement Learning from Images For Transfer) are remarkably streamlined.

### IV-A RL Algorithm and Policy Architecture
Training relies on GPU-parallelized PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). A central feature is the asymmetric Critic $v_{\psi}(s_{t}^{\mathrm{priv}})$, which accesses privileged simulation states $s_{t}^{\mathrm{priv}}$ exclusively during training. This leverages privileged information to stabilize value estimation, while the Actor (policy) deployed at test time only receives physical camera images and proprioception. The Actor backbone is a lightweight 3-layer Encoder-only Transformer with a hidden dimension of 64, processing proprioceptive tokens and visual tokens together through shared self-attention layers.

### IV-B Frozen Visual Features and Attention Pooling
The core design choice is freezing (stop-gradient) the vision encoder $f_{\phi}$ (such as DINOv3 ViT-S/16). This avoids backpropagation through the vision backbone and allows caching image features across multiple PPO update epochs ($K$ updates per rollout). As a result, forward passes through the encoder drop to $1/K$, dramatically boosting the number of environment steps collected and processed per wall-clock hour.

Furthermore, because the strong visual representations pretrained on natural images remain intact, they transfer zero-shot to physical camera frames even when trained on fast, rasterized simulation renders. Costly ray-traced rendering is not required.

However, using only the [CLS] token (global image summary) discards local spatial details needed for millimeter-precise contact manipulation. Conversely, feeding all patch tokens directly into the Transformer policy triggers a quadratic explosion in compute. Drift solves this by introducing Multihead Attention Pooling (MAP), which compresses patch tokens into a small set of learned query vectors. This successfully preserves spatial resolution while keeping downstream computational costs minimal.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: Three manipulation tasks and rigorous OOD testing
sections.summary: Evaluations span three tasks: Pick-Cube, Push-T, and high-precision Peg-Insertion. Implemented in ManiSkill, the benchmark systematically evaluates out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness against shifts in object mass, goal locations, camera poses, and external disturbance forces.
sections.details:
To evaluate Drift's real-world efficacy, rigorous comparative experiments were conducted across simulation and a physical Franka Research 3 robot arm.

### V-A Target Tasks
Three distinct manipulation tasks were chosen to cover diverse challenges:
- **Pick-Cube**: A foundational task requiring grasping and lifting a cube.
- **Push-T**: A non-prehensile manipulation task requiring pushing a T-shaped block to align accurately with a visually indicated goal template.
- **Peg-Insertion**: A precision-demanding, contact-rich task of inserting a peg into a square hole with only 2 mm of clearance.

### V-B Training Environment and Domain Randomization
The policy was trained in the ManiSkill parallel simulator, outputting 8-dimensional continuous commands at 20 Hz (relative joint position targets and gripper command). To facilitate sim-to-real transfer, object friction, textures, lighting (HDR environment maps), and camera extrinsics were systematically randomized, with backgrounds composited from a curated pool of roughly 27,000 natural images.

### V-C Evaluation Protocol
To ensure a fair comparison, both Drift and two-phase distillation were allocated identical computational budgets on NVIDIA L40S GPUs (roughly 150 GPU hours each). Periodic evaluations of 1,024 simulation episodes identified the top checkpoint per seed. After 5 screening trials on the physical robot, the best models were selected and evaluated over 20 to 30 full real-world trials, measuring both success rate and throughput (completed tasks per unit time).

sections.heading: Results: Comparable in simulation, decisive in the real world and OOD
sections.summary: While the performance gap was only ~9% under in-distribution (ID) simulation, Drift's advantage expanded to 61% under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. In real-world transfer, Drift achieved a 58.8% average relative improvement and generalized well to novel objects with unseen geometries.
sections.details:
The experimental findings provide clear, compelling takeaways.

### VI-A In-Simulation Generalization and Distribution Shifts
First, policies were benchmarked in simulation across in-distribution (ID) conditions and out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. The four OOD perturbations included altered object mass (up to 4x) and scale, expanded goal regions, camera pose offsets (24-pixel translation), and external disturbance forces applied to the gripper (80 N).
In the ID setup, Drift outperformed distillation by an 8.6% relative margin—a modest difference. However, under OOD shifts, two-phase distillation suffered a ~42% performance drop, whereas Drift degraded by only 14%. Consequently, Drift's relative lead surged to 61% under OOD conditions. In the expanded goal region experiment, distillation degraded steeply outside the training bounds, while Drift maintained high success rates over a much broader area.

### VI-B Real-World Zero-Shot Transfer
When transferred directly to physical hardware, the performance gap became even more pronounced. In the challenging Peg-Insertion task, two-phase distillation with a frozen ViT dropped to a 23.3% success rate, whereas Drift achieved 66.7%. The sim-to-real drop for distillation was 55.2 percentage points, compared to just 15.7 points for Drift. In Push-T, Drift dominated with 76.7% against distillation's 30.0%. Across all three tasks, Drift delivered an average relative improvement of 58.8% in real-world success.
Furthermore, when testing the Pick-Cube policy (trained only on a single black cube) on four novel objects—a red cube, a cylinder, an oversized cube, and a Rubik's cube—distillation's success fell to 50.0%, while Drift maintained an 88.8% success rate.
Analyzing the log-likelihood of internal policy latent representations during physical deployment revealed that Drift's activations remained significantly closer to its simulation distribution. Policies trained with direct RL inherently learn closed-loop recovery behaviors that stay resilient despite visual and physical sim-to-real discrepancies.

### VI-C Selecting the Optimal Vision Encoder
Comparing seven vision backbones across ViT, CNN, DINOv3, SigLIP2, and ImageNet pretraining, DINOv3 ViT-S/16 achieved the top performance in both simulation (82.2%) and physical execution (66.7%). Notably, models like SigLIP2 and ConvNeXt-B scored above 70% in simulation, but collapsed to 3.3%–10.0% on the physical robot. This highlights an important lesson: larger parameter counts and high in-simulation scores do not necessarily translate to effective real-world transfer.

captions.F5: Comparison of task success rates between in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) simulation settings. Across object mass/scale, goal positions, camera pose shifts, and disturbance forces, two-phase distillation experiences sharp drops under OOD conditions (hatched bars), whereas Drift retains high success rates.
captions.F6: Goal position generalization maps for Push-T (top) and Peg-Insertion (bottom). The black center box marks the training region. Drift (left) sustains high success rates across a much wider spatial area, even far beyond the training boundary.
captions.F7: Zero-shot transfer results on novel physical objects (red cube, cylinder, oversized cube, and Rubik's cube) using policies trained exclusively on a plain black cube. Even with drastic shifts in geometry and surface texture, Drift maintains substantially higher success rates than distillation.

sections.heading: Takeaway: One-phase direct RL is enough for Sim-to-Real transfer
sections.summary: By pairing frozen vision foundation models with Attention Pooling and fast simulation rendering, one-phase visual RL without privileged teacher distillation proves highly practical. The superior generalization of direct RL has the potential to reshape standard recipes for robot vision control.
sections.details:
The message of "Drift" is clear and decisive: you do not need a two-phase distillation pipeline through a privileged teacher to acquire robust visual policies for sim-to-real transfer. With the right recipe, one-phase direct visual RL is not only sufficient, but vastly superior in the real world.

By delegating feature extraction to a frozen vision encoder pretrained on massive web-scale images and training only a lightweight downstream Transformer policy with RL, the approach bypasses heavy encoder backpropagation and costly ray-traced rendering. This frees up GPU resources to focus almost entirely on high-throughput trial-and-error environment interactions.

Most importantly, the paper cautions against judging visual policies by in-distribution simulation metrics alone. Even when distillation matches direct RL in simulation benchmarks, policies learned directly from outcome-based task returns display far greater resilience when encountering physical domain gaps, out-of-distribution shifts, and novel objects. Moving away from teacher imitation toward foundation-model-anchored direct RL provides a formidable new baseline for robotic manipulation research.

takeaways: Imitation distillation from privileged teachers often produces an illusion of capability, achieving high in-simulation scores while collapsing under real-world domain shifts.
Freezing pretrained ViTs (such as DINOv3) eliminates expensive ray tracing and heavy backpropagation, enabling zero-shot real-world transfer directly from fast rasterized simulation renders.
For precision manipulation, aggregating spatial tokens via Multihead Attention Pooling (MAP) is vastly superior to relying solely on the global [CLS] token.
Controlled evaluations under intentional out-of-distribution (OOD) perturbations are critical for accurately predicting real-world transfer success, whereas in-distribution metrics can be misleading.
limitations: Transfer performance is heavily dependent on the chosen pretrained vision backbone, and the theoretical reasons why certain models (e.g., DINOv3 vs. SigLIP2) yield drastically different real-world transfer rates remain incompletely understood.

Experiments primarily focus on single-arm setups with wrist-mounted cameras; validating the setup across multi-view static camera configurations and long-horizon, multi-task settings remains future work.
Simulation background substitution and texture randomization (domain randomization) still require manual tuning and engineering, meaning the recipe is not entirely hyperparameter-free.
